United States.0: The first people crossed from Asia via Beringia by at least c. 15,000 years ago. Clovis hunters later stalked mammoths and bison, but after the Ice Age the big game vanished, and Archaic hunter-gatherers adapted to local forests, plains, deserts and coasts, moving north into Canada as the glaciers retreated.
United States.1: Archaic hunter-gatherers lived across North America in small bands, fishing, gathering nuts and hunting deer. In the Southeast, people piled up shell rings and mounds, and eastern groups began tending local seed plants like sunflower and squash. Paleo-Eskimo peoples spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Canada and Greenland.
United States.2: Around c. 1700 BC, people at Poverty Point in Louisiana built huge earthen ridges and mounds and traded for stone and copper from far away, all without farming. Maize had reached the Southwest by c. 2000 BC, while eastern foragers were domesticating native seed crops such as goosefoot and sumpweed.
United States.3: The Early Woodland era began in the East, bringing pottery, more settled villages and the first burial mounds of the Adena culture in the Ohio Valley. In the Southwest, early farmers dug irrigation canals for maize. In the Arctic, the Dorset culture took shape among hunters of seal and caribou.
United States.4: No states existed; hundreds of independent peoples lived by hunting, fishing, gathering and some gardening. The Adena of the Ohio Valley buried honored dead in earthen mounds with copper and mica ornaments. Pacific Northwest peoples relied on salmon, and Southwest farmers combined maize with wild foods.
United States.5: Adena communities kept building burial mounds and trading goods such as Great Lakes copper and Gulf Coast shells. On the Plains, bison hunters moved with the herds, while in California dense populations lived on acorns and seafood without needing to farm. Life remained village-based and kin-centered.
United States.6: Across the continent, regional ways of life grew more distinct. Late Adena peoples in the Ohio Valley built ever larger mounds, Basketmaker farmers on the Colorado Plateau grew maize and squash and wove fine baskets, and Northwest Coast villagers built plank houses and stored dried salmon for winter.
United States.7: The Hopewell tradition began to emerge in Ohio and Illinois around c. 200 BC. Its people built large geometric earthworks and joined a vast exchange network carrying obsidian, copper, shells and mica. Elsewhere, foragers and small-scale farmers continued long-established ways of life.
United States.8: Hopewell culture grew in the Midwest, with ceremonial centers where people gathered for feasts, burials and trade. Its craftsmen made copper ornaments, mica cutouts and carved stone pipes. Related mound traditions such as Marksville appeared in the lower Mississippi Valley.
United States.9: The Hopewell Interaction Sphere linked communities from the Rockies to the Atlantic coast through shared rituals and long-distance trade. In the Southwest, farming villages were growing, and in the far north Dorset peoples hunted sea mammals across Arctic Canada.
United States.10: Hopewell societies flourished, building giant earthworks such as those at Newark, Ohio, aligned with the movements of the Moon. In the deserts of southern Arizona, the ancestors of the Hohokam were beginning to farm with irrigation. Most people still lived in small villages or mobile bands.
United States.11: Hopewell ceremonial life was at its height in the Ohio and Illinois valleys. In the Southwest, early Mogollon and Basketmaker communities lived in pithouse villages and farmed maize. Northwest Coast societies grew richer and more ranked, with chiefs, nobles and commoners.
United States.12: Hopewell centers continued to draw people for rituals and trade. Mogollon villages took shape in the mountains of New Mexico and Arizona, making some of the region's earliest pottery. Across the Plains and Great Basin, mobile foragers followed the seasons.
United States.13: Hopewell mound-building and long-distance trade began to fade, for reasons that are still debated. Hohokam farmers in Arizona extended irrigation canals along the Salt and Gila rivers. Across the East, people relied more on gardens of native seed crops alongside hunting and gathering.
United States.14: The Hopewell era ended and the Late Woodland period began, with smaller, more scattered communities. The bow and arrow spread across much of the continent, changing hunting and warfare. In the Southwest, Basketmaker peoples adopted pottery and beans.
United States.15: Late Woodland peoples lived in villages across the East, increasingly using the bow and arrow. Basketmaker communities on the Colorado Plateau built pithouse villages and stored maize in pots. Hohokam towns in Arizona grew around expanding canal networks.
United States.16: In the Upper Midwest, Effigy Mound peoples began shaping earthen mounds into birds, bears and other animals. In Arkansas, the Plum Bayou culture built the Toltec Mounds center. Southwestern farmers were becoming more dependent on maize.
United States.17: Ancestral Puebloans in the Four Corners began building above-ground, multi-room pueblos, while the Hohokam built ball courts and miles of canals. In the East, maize farming started to spread, supporting larger villages. Effigy mounds still rose in Wisconsin and Iowa.
United States.18: In Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, Ancestral Puebloans started building multi-story great houses such as Pueblo Bonito. In the Mississippi Valley, maize-farming communities were laying the foundations of the Mississippian culture. Hohokam society thrived in the Arizona desert.
United States.19: Chaco Canyon grew into a regional center linked by long straight roads and trade in turquoise and macaws. Along the Mississippi and its tributaries, maize-based chiefdoms took shape. In the 980s, Norse settlers from Iceland reached Greenland, on the eastern edge of the Arctic world.
United States.20: Around c. 1050, Cahokia near modern St. Louis burst into a planned city of perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, the largest north of Mexico. Chaco Canyon reached its peak. The Norse briefly camped at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, and Thule Inuit began moving east from Alaska.
United States.21: Cahokia was at its height, with the giant Monks Mound and a powerful elite. Mississippian chiefdoms spread across the Southeast, including Moundville in Alabama and Etowah in Georgia. Drought brought Chaco's decline, and Puebloans built new cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde.
United States.22: Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings flourished until a great drought late in the century drove Puebloans out of the Four Corners. Cahokia began to shrink, while Moundville, Spiro and Etowah thrived. Thule Inuit, ancestors of today's Inuit, spread across Arctic Canada to Greenland.
United States.23: Cahokia was largely abandoned by c. 1350, and Puebloans resettled along the Rio Grande and at Hopi and Zuni. Mississippian chiefdoms shared a striking religious art style across the Southeast. In the Northeast, Iroquoian peoples lived in fortified villages of longhouses, farming maize, beans and squash.
United States.24: Millions of people lived in what is now the US and Canada, in hundreds of nations. Mississippian chiefdoms such as Coosa ruled the Southeast, the Hohokam system collapsed, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy may have formed in this era. In 1497, John Cabot reached Newfoundland.
United States.25: Europeans arrived: Ponce de León reached Florida in 1513, de Soto and Coronado marched through the Southeast and Southwest, and Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565. In Canada, Cartier explored the St. Lawrence. Above all, European diseases devastated Native nations, often ahead of the Europeans themselves.
United States.26: England planted colonies at Jamestown (1607) and Plymouth (1620), and enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619. France founded Quebec, the Dutch New Amsterdam. Native nations fought back in wars such as King Philip's War and the 1680 Pueblo Revolt as settlers took their land.
United States.27: British colonies grew fast along the Atlantic coast, with Georgia founded in 1732, and enslaved Africans worked tobacco and rice plantations in the South. The Great Awakening stirred colonial religion. France held Canada and Louisiana, Spain held Florida and Texas, and the Comanche rose to power on the southern Plains.
United States.28: Britain won the French and Indian War (1754 to 1763), taking Canada, but its new taxes sparked revolution. The colonies declared independence in 1776, won it by the 1783 Treaty of Paris, and wrote the Constitution in 1787. Native nations lost land as settlers pushed west.
United States.29: The young republic doubled its size with the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, sent Lewis and Clark west, and fought Britain in the War of 1812, when invasions of Canada failed. The 1823 Monroe Doctrine warned Europe off the Americas. Cotton and slavery spread across the Deep South.
United States.30: Under the 1830 Indian Removal Act, the Cherokee and other nations were forced west on the Trail of Tears. The US annexed Texas and took the Southwest in the Mexican-American War, and the 1849 Gold Rush drew crowds to California. Arguments over slavery's expansion intensified.
United States.31: The fight over slavery led to the Civil War (1861 to 1865), which killed about 620,000 to 750,000 people. The Union won, slavery ended with the 13th Amendment, and Reconstruction began. The transcontinental railroad opened in 1869, and Canada became a self-governing confederation in 1867.
United States.32: Reconstruction ended in 1877 and Jim Crow segregation took hold in the South. In the Gilded Age, railroads, steel and oil made the US an industrial giant, and millions of immigrants arrived. Plains nations were confined to reservations, and the 1898 Spanish-American War brought an overseas empire.
United States.33: In the Progressive Era, reformers under presidents like Theodore Roosevelt tackled monopolies, corruption and unsafe food. Immigration peaked through Ellis Island, cities grew, and the Wright brothers flew in 1903. The US began building the Panama Canal and acted as a regional police power.
United States.34: Henry Ford's assembly line made cars affordable, and new laws created the Federal Reserve and the income tax. The US entered World War I in 1917, emerging as a creditor nation. The Great Migration took Black Southerners north, and the 1918 flu killed hundreds of thousands.
United States.35: Women won the vote with the 19th Amendment in 1920. The Roaring Twenties brought jazz, radio, movies and booming stock prices, alongside Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance and strict new limits on immigration. The decade ended with the stock market crash of 1929.
United States.36: The Great Depression left a quarter of workers jobless, and the Dust Bowl drove farm families off the Plains. Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal from 1933 created Social Security, public works jobs and banking regulations, greatly expanding the federal government.
United States.37: Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 brought the US into World War II, and its factories armed the Allies. The war ended with atomic bombs on Japan in 1945, leaving the US a superpower. The 1948 Marshall Plan and NATO opened the Cold War with the Soviet Union.
United States.38: Postwar prosperity built suburbs, interstate highways and a baby boom, while the Korean War and McCarthyism reflected Cold War fears. The 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling struck down school segregation, and the Montgomery bus boycott launched the Civil Rights Movement.
United States.39: President Kennedy was assassinated in 1963. The Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act of 1964 and 1965 ended legal segregation, but Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in 1968 amid war protests and urban unrest over Vietnam. In 1969, Apollo 11 landed astronauts on the Moon.
United States.40: The US left Vietnam in 1973, and President Nixon resigned in 1974 over the Watergate scandal. Oil shocks brought inflation and slow growth, shaking confidence. The decade also saw the Roe v. Wade abortion ruling, the rise of environmentalism and new women's rights laws.
United States.41: Ronald Reagan cut taxes, deregulated business and built up the military, taking a hard line against the Soviet Union. The economy recovered from inflation, and personal computers spread. By 1989, the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War was ending.
United States.42: With the Soviet collapse in 1991, the US became the world's sole superpower and led the Gulf War. NAFTA linked it to Canada and Mexico, and the internet fueled a dot-com boom and budget surpluses under President Clinton.
United States.43: The 9/11 attacks in 2001 led to wars in Afghanistan and, from 2003, Iraq. A housing bubble burst into the 2008 financial crisis, the worst downturn since the Depression. That same year, Barack Obama was elected the first Black president.
United States.44: The economy slowly recovered, the Affordable Care Act expanded health insurance, and the Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage nationwide in 2015. Smartphones and social media reshaped daily life. Political polarization deepened, and Donald Trump won the presidency in 2016.
United States.45: COVID-19 killed more than 1 million Americans. After Joe Biden won the 2020 election, a mob stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and the US withdrew from Afghanistan that year. Inflation surged, and Donald Trump returned to the presidency in 2025.

Mexico.0: Hunter-gatherers lived in Mexico by the end of the Ice Age. In the highlands of Oaxaca and the Balsas Valley, Archaic foragers began domesticating squash and then maize, bred from the wild grass teosinte by c. 7000 BC. Beans and chili peppers followed, laying the foundation of Mesoamerican life.
Mexico.1: Archaic peoples still moved seasonally, but maize cobs were slowly growing larger and gardens mattered more. Toward the end of this era, the first pottery and more permanent settlements appeared along the Pacific and Gulf coasts, setting the stage for village life.
Mexico.2: Farming villages spread across Mesoamerica. From c. 1500 BC, the Olmecs of the Gulf Coast built San Lorenzo, carved colossal stone heads and shaped Mesoamerica's 'mother culture,' with its rulers, jade, ballgame and jaguar imagery. Villages like Tlatilco and San José Mogote grew in the highlands.
Mexico.3: The Olmec center of La Venta in Tabasco rose to prominence with an earthen pyramid, colossal heads and buried offerings of jade. In Oaxaca, San José Mogote grew into a ranked chiefdom. Olmec styles spread widely through trade, showing a world of growing chiefs and ceremonial centers.
Mexico.4: Around c. 500 BC, the Zapotecs founded Monte Albán on a hilltop in Oaxaca, which became one of Mesoamerica's first true cities and an early center of writing and calendars. Olmec La Venta was in its late phase, and Maya villages were growing in Chiapas and Yucatán.
Mexico.5: La Venta declined around c. 400 BC, and the classic Olmec era came to an end. Monte Albán grew as the capital of a Zapotec state, carving stone monuments of conquered captives. In the Valley of Mexico, Cuicuilco built a round pyramid and became the region's leading town.
Mexico.6: After the Olmecs, Epi-Olmec communities such as Tres Zapotes carried their traditions on along the Gulf Coast. The Zapotec state of Monte Albán expanded across Oaxaca, and Izapa in Chiapas carved story-telling stone monuments. Populations rose as farming intensified.
Mexico.7: Rival towns competed in the Valley of Mexico, led by Cuicuilco. In the north of the valley, settlement began at Teotihuacan. Monte Albán dominated Oaxaca, and in West Mexico people buried their dead in deep shaft tombs filled with lively clay figures.
Mexico.8: Teotihuacan grew rapidly as people moved there from across the Valley of Mexico. Monte Albán ruled much of Oaxaca, and Maya cities were growing in the Yucatán. Writing and the calendar were spreading through Mesoamerica.
Mexico.9: At Tres Zapotes on the Gulf Coast, Stela C bears a date equivalent to 32 BC, one of the earliest known Long Count dates. Teotihuacan was becoming the Valley of Mexico's dominant city, while Cuicuilco faded. Monte Albán continued to rule Oaxaca.
Mexico.10: Teotihuacan began its great construction projects, laying out a grid aligned on the Avenue of the Dead. Its people farmed the valley, worked obsidian and drew migrants from afar. Monte Albán ruled Oaxaca, and West Mexico's shaft-tomb cultures flourished.
Mexico.11: Teotihuacan became one of the world's largest cities, peaking at perhaps 100,000 people between c. 100 and 550. Its builders raised the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. The city's influence spread through trade in obsidian and fine goods across Mesoamerica.
Mexico.12: Teotihuacan completed the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, burying sacrificial victims beneath it. Residents lived in large apartment compounds, including neighborhoods of Zapotec and Gulf Coast migrants. In the Maya lowlands of southern Mexico, Calakmul and other cities entered the Classic era.
Mexico.13: Teotihuacan's reach extended deep into the Maya world; in 378 its agents helped install a new dynasty at Tikal. At home, the city's rulers stayed strikingly anonymous in its art. Monte Albán remained Oaxaca's capital, and Maya kingdoms grew in Campeche and Chiapas.
Mexico.14: Teotihuacan was at the height of its power, a cosmopolitan city of artisans, traders and priests. Monte Albán thrived as Teotihuacan's partner in Oaxaca. In the Maya lowlands of southern Mexico, Calakmul's Snake dynasty and Palenque were rising.
Mexico.15: Around c. 550, Teotihuacan's center was burned and the great city collapsed, perhaps through internal revolt. Its fall broke central Mexico into smaller rival states. In the south, the Maya kingdoms of Calakmul and Palenque flourished.
Mexico.16: In the Epiclassic era after Teotihuacan, new centers rose: Cholula, Xochicalco, Cacaxtla and El Tajín on the Gulf Coast. At Palenque, King Pakal the Great (ruled 615 to 683) built splendid temples, and Calakmul fought Tikal for supremacy in the Maya world.
Mexico.17: Fortified hilltop cities like Xochicalco competed for trade in central Mexico, and El Tajín's ballcourts flourished in Veracruz. Monte Albán gradually lost its power over Oaxaca. Late in the century, the Classic Maya cities of the south began to falter.
Mexico.18: The Classic Maya kingdoms of Chiapas and Campeche collapsed, but in the northern Yucatán Puuc cities like Uxmal flourished and Chichén Itzá rose. In central Mexico, the Toltecs began building their capital at Tula. Power was shifting north.
Mexico.19: The Toltecs, ruling from Tula in Hidalgo, became central Mexico's dominant power, remembered later as master craftsmen and warriors. In the Yucatán, Chichén Itzá rose to dominate the north, with art that shares striking Toltec-style features. Trade routes stretched to the American Southwest.
Mexico.20: Tula was at its peak, with warrior columns and a far-reaching trade network. Chichén Itzá ruled much of Yucatán. In Oaxaca, Mixtec kingdoms flourished; the famous lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw (1063 to 1115) united many of them through conquest and marriage.
Mexico.21: Tula fell around c. 1150 and was burned, ending Toltec power. Waves of northern peoples, called Chichimecs, migrated into central Mexico, among them the Mexica, later known as the Aztecs. Chichén Itzá declined, and the Mixtecs produced fine codices and goldwork.
Mexico.22: Central Mexico was divided among rival city-states such as Azcapotzalco and Culhuacan. The wandering Mexica arrived in the Valley of Mexico, serving as mercenaries. In Yucatán, Mayapán became the leading city, and in Michoacán the Purépecha (Tarascans) began to build their state.
Mexico.23: In 1325, the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, building chinampa farm plots in the lake. They served the powerful Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco while growing stronger. The Tarascans built a rival kingdom at Tzintzuntzan, and Mayapán ruled Yucatán.
Mexico.24: In 1428, the Aztec Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan overthrew the Tepanecs and built a tribute empire across central and southern Mexico. Tenochtitlan grew to perhaps 200,000 people. The Tarascans defeated the Aztecs c. 1478, and Mayapán fell in the mid-1400s.
Mexico.25: Hernán Cortés and Indigenous allies such as Tlaxcala conquered the Aztecs in 1519 to 1521, aided by smallpox. Spain built Mexico City on the ruins and created New Spain. Epidemics killed most of the Native population, while silver mines at Zacatecas began to enrich the empire.
Mexico.26: New Spain was a prosperous Spanish colony whose silver, shipped via the Manila galleons, linked Europe and Asia. Haciendas and mines relied on Indigenous and African labor, and a mixed society of castas grew. The Native population hit its low point early in the century and slowly recovered.
Mexico.27: Under the new Bourbon kings of Spain, New Spain's silver output rose and lavish Baroque churches were built. Mestizos became a growing share of the population. Spain founded missions and presidios in Texas to block French expansion from Louisiana.
Mexico.28: The Bourbon Reforms tightened Spanish control and taxes, expelled the Jesuits in 1767, and favored Spanish-born officials over Mexican-born Creoles. Missions spread into California from 1769. Guanajuato's silver mines became the world's richest, but resentment of Spain grew.
Mexico.29: In 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo launched a revolt against Spanish rule, followed by José María Morelos. Both were executed, but in 1821 Agustín de Iturbide won independence and briefly made himself emperor. In 1824, Mexico became a federal republic.
Mexico.30: Mexico struggled with coups and debts, led on and off by Antonio López de Santa Anna. Texas broke away in 1836. In the Mexican-American War (1846 to 1848), Mexico lost about half its territory to the US, and the Caste War erupted among the Maya of Yucatán.
Mexico.31: Liberals led by Benito Juárez passed reforms limiting the Church's power, sparking the Reform War (1858 to 1861). France then invaded and installed Emperor Maximilian (1864 to 1867), but Juárez's forces defeated and executed him, restoring the republic.
Mexico.32: Porfirio Díaz ruled as a dictator from 1876 to 1911, bringing order, railroads and foreign investment. Mexico modernized, but land became concentrated in a few hands, and peasants and Indigenous peoples such as the Yaqui lost their lands. Dissent was suppressed.
Mexico.33: Díaz's regime looked stable but grew brittle as he aged. Foreign companies owned mines, railways and newly discovered oil fields, and strikes at Cananea (1906) and Río Blanco (1907) were crushed. In 1910, Francisco Madero challenged Díaz's re-election.
Mexico.34: The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) toppled Díaz and became a bloody civil war among leaders like Madero, Huerta, Villa, Zapata and Carranza, killing perhaps a million or more people. The US intervened twice. The 1917 Constitution promised land reform and workers' rights.
Mexico.35: Revolutionary generals Obregón and Calles rebuilt the state, while muralists like Diego Rivera celebrated Mexico's Indigenous past. Anticlerical laws sparked the Cristero War (1926 to 1929). In 1929, Calles founded the party that would later become the PRI.
Mexico.36: President Lázaro Cárdenas (1934 to 1940) redistributed millions of acres of land to peasants, backed labor unions and in 1938 nationalized the oil industry, creating Pemex. These reforms made him a national hero and cemented the ruling party's grip.
Mexico.37: Mexico joined the Allies in World War II, and the Bracero Program sent Mexican workers to US farms. The ruling party took the name PRI in 1946. Industrial growth began the 'Mexican Miracle,' and cities expanded rapidly.
Mexico.38: The 'Mexican Miracle' brought steady growth, new factories and a booming middle class, all under the PRI's one-party rule. Women gained the right to vote in federal elections in 1953. Mexico City grew into a sprawling metropolis.
Mexico.39: Growth continued, but resentment of PRI authoritarianism rose. Days before Mexico City hosted the 1968 Olympics, troops killed protesting students at Tlatelolco. The massacre shattered the image of a stable, democratic Mexico.
Mexico.40: Presidents Echeverría and López Portillo spent heavily and borrowed abroad, especially after huge offshore oil fields were found in the late 1970s. Security forces fought a 'dirty war' against leftist guerrillas. Oil wealth hid deep economic problems.
Mexico.41: Falling oil prices brought the 1982 debt crisis, and the peso collapsed. The 1985 Mexico City earthquake killed thousands and exposed government failings. The PRI's disputed 1988 election victory sparked protests, and Mexico began opening its economy.
Mexico.42: NAFTA took effect in 1994, the same day the Zapatistas rose up in Chiapas for Indigenous rights. A peso crisis followed. Political reforms loosened the PRI's grip, and it lost control of Congress in 1997.
Mexico.43: In 2000, Vicente Fox's victory ended the PRI's 71-year rule. In 2006, President Felipe Calderón sent the army against drug cartels, launching a drug war that brought soaring violence. Mexico's economy grew more tightly tied to the US through manufacturing.
Mexico.44: Cartel violence continued, and the disappearance of 43 students from Ayotzinapa in 2014 provoked outrage. Enrique Peña Nieto brought back the PRI and opened the oil sector. In 2018, the leftist Andrés Manuel López Obrador won a landslide.
Mexico.45: López Obrador expanded social programs and the army's role, while COVID-19 killed hundreds of thousands. In 2024, Claudia Sheinbaum was elected Mexico's first woman president. Mexico became the United States' largest trading partner, though tariffs and migration strained ties.

Caribbean.0: For most of this era the islands were empty of people. Foragers reached Trinidad, then close to South America, by c. 6000 BC, and canoe voyagers, perhaps from Central America, reached Cuba and Hispaniola by c. 4000 BC. These Archaic peoples fished, gathered shellfish and hunted with stone tools.
Caribbean.1: Small Archaic bands lived on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, while others island-hopped north from Trinidad into the Lesser Antilles. They had no pottery or farming to speak of, living from the sea, mangroves and forests, and some islands remained unsettled.
Caribbean.2: Archaic foragers continued to live along island coasts, leaving shell middens and ground stone tools. Some may have tended wild plants and fruit trees, moving useful species between islands. Population stayed small, scattered in kin-based groups without chiefs or towns.
Caribbean.3: Island life remained largely unchanged: Archaic peoples fished from canoes, collected shellfish and hunted small animals such as hutias. Several islands, including Jamaica and the Bahamas, still had no human settlers. On the South American mainland, farming peoples were preparing to move into the islands.
Caribbean.4: Around c. 500 BC, the Saladoid people, farmers and potters from the Orinoco region of Venezuela, began paddling up the Lesser Antilles into Puerto Rico. They brought cassava (manioc) farming and beautiful white-on-red pottery, settling in permanent villages near the older Archaic foragers.
Caribbean.5: Saladoid villagers spread through the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico, clearing gardens for cassava and sweet potatoes. A related group, the Huecoid, also lived in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Archaic foragers continued to occupy Cuba and Hispaniola.
Caribbean.6: Saladoid communities lived in circular villages arranged around central plazas, where they buried their dead. They made fine pottery and carved amulets from imported stones. Islands were linked by canoe trade to each other and to the South American mainland.
Caribbean.7: Saladoid farmers and Archaic foragers shared the islands, sometimes trading. Villages were organized around extended families and spiritual leaders, and early zemí-like carved objects suggest shared religious beliefs. Cassava bread baked on clay griddles became a staple.
Caribbean.8: Saladoid culture thrived from Trinidad to eastern Hispaniola. Villages grew larger, and long-distance exchange brought stones such as jadeite and carnelian into the islands. Most people lived from gardens, fishing and collecting shellfish.
Caribbean.9: The Saladoid way of life remained stable for centuries, with farming villages throughout the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico. Pottery decorated with modeled animals and painted patterns reflected a rich mythology. Archaic peoples still held much of Cuba.
Caribbean.10: Saladoid societies were at their height, with large villages in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Communities shared rituals and burial customs, and canoe routes connected many islands. Life remained village-based, without kingdoms or cities.
Caribbean.11: Saladoid villagers continued farming cassava, fishing and trading by canoe. Their art showed animals such as frogs, bats and turtles that held religious meaning. Archaic foragers continued older ways in the western islands.
Caribbean.12: Caribbean societies changed slowly. Saladoid villages dotted the eastern islands, while Archaic foragers lived in Cuba and parts of Hispaniola. Shell, stone and pottery crafts flourished, and village plazas served as ceremonial spaces.
Caribbean.13: The Saladoid world remained stable, with dozens of farming villages across the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico. Some communities began to show signs of ranking, with certain families gaining status. Canoe trade continued to knit islands together.
Caribbean.14: Late Saladoid pottery became simpler as local styles diverged from island to island. Populations grew in Puerto Rico and eastern Hispaniola. These changes set the stage for new cultures that would take shape over the next centuries.
Caribbean.15: The Saladoid era was drawing to a close as local traditions developed in Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Farming communities expanded inland, and some villages grew larger and more permanent. Archaic peoples still lived in Cuba.
Caribbean.16: Around c. 600, the Ostionoid culture emerged from Saladoid roots in Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Ostionoid farmers soon spread west to settle Jamaica for the first time and moved into eastern Cuba. Their villages were larger, and farming more intensive.
Caribbean.17: Ostionoid farmers settled the Bahamas, where their descendants became the Lucayans, and expanded across Hispaniola and Cuba. They built mounded fields for cassava. Chiefs were gaining power as populations grew.
Caribbean.18: Ostionoid societies grew denser, and the first stone-lined ball courts and plazas appeared in Puerto Rico. These spaces were used for ballgames, dances and ceremonies. Village chiefs began to form larger alliances.
Caribbean.19: Chiefdoms grew larger and more organized in Hispaniola and Puerto Rico. Ballgames, ancestor worship and carved stone collars and zemís became important parts of religious and political life. The islands were becoming one of the most densely populated areas in the Americas.
Caribbean.20: The Taíno culture took shape in Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Cuba and Jamaica. Chiefs called caciques ruled villages and districts, and communities farmed cassava in mounds called conucos. In the Lesser Antilles, distinct island cultures developed.
Caribbean.21: Taíno chiefdoms expanded, with powerful caciques controlling multiple villages and receiving tribute. Religious life centered on zemís, spirit images carved in stone and wood. In the Lesser Antilles, ancestors of the Kalinago (Island Caribs) were living, though their origins are debated.
Caribbean.22: Taíno society reached a high level of complexity, with large ceremonial centers like Caguana in Puerto Rico, featuring stone-lined plazas and petroglyphs. Hispaniola was divided among several major chiefdoms. The Kalinago lived in the Lesser Antilles.
Caribbean.23: Taíno chiefdoms dominated the Greater Antilles, with a population that may have reached several hundred thousand or more. Large canoes carried trade and warriors between islands. The Lucayans of the Bahamas and the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles had their own distinct cultures.
Caribbean.24: The Taíno lived in prosperous chiefdoms across the Greater Antilles. In 1492, Columbus landed in the Bahamas and Hispaniola, beginning European contact. Spain built its first settlement, La Isabela, in 1493, and soon began demanding gold and labor from the Taíno.
Caribbean.25: Under Spanish rule, the Taíno population collapsed from war, forced labor and disease. Spain founded Santo Domingo, Havana and San Juan, then turned to sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Pirates and privateers from rival nations began raiding Spanish ports.
Caribbean.26: English, French and Dutch forces seized islands, including Barbados and Jamaica (1655), while France took western Hispaniola. A sugar boom built on African slavery transformed the islands into plantation colonies. Buccaneers based at Port Royal and Tortuga ushered in the golden age of piracy.
Caribbean.27: Sugar made the Caribbean the most valuable part of the colonial world, with Saint-Domingue becoming the richest colony on earth. Enslaved Africans made up the vast majority of people, enduring brutal conditions. Jamaica's Maroons won a treaty from Britain in 1739, and piracy was suppressed.
Caribbean.28: Britain briefly captured Havana in 1762 during the Seven Years' War. In 1791, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up, beginning the Haitian Revolution under leaders like Toussaint Louverture. They abolished slavery and defeated French, Spanish and British forces.
Caribbean.29: In 1804, Haiti became the first independent Black republic, born of a successful slave revolt. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, while Cuba's sugar plantations expanded with enslaved labor. Haiti took control of Spanish Santo Domingo in 1822.
Caribbean.30: Britain freed the enslaved people in its Caribbean colonies between 1834 and 1838, and France followed in 1848. The Dominican Republic broke from Haiti in 1844, while Haiti struggled under a crushing indemnity demanded by France in 1825. Indentured laborers from India began arriving in Trinidad.
Caribbean.31: Cuba's sugar wealth still depended on slavery, and its Ten Years' War for independence began in 1868. Spain reoccupied the Dominican Republic from 1861 to 1865. Jamaica's Morant Bay Rebellion in 1865 was brutally crushed, and Puerto Rico abolished slavery in 1873.
Caribbean.32: Cuba abolished slavery in 1886, and José Martí launched a new independence war in 1895. In 1898, the US intervened in the Spanish-American War and took Cuba and Puerto Rico. The British colonies remained poor, dependent on falling sugar prices.
Caribbean.33: Cuba became independent in 1902 but under US control through the Platt Amendment, which granted the US Guantánamo Bay. Puerto Rico was governed directly as a US territory. In 1902, Mount Pelée's eruption on Martinique killed about 28,000 people.
Caribbean.34: The US occupied Haiti (1915 to 1934) and the Dominican Republic (1916 to 1924), and bought the Danish Virgin Islands in 1917. Puerto Ricans became US citizens in 1917. A World War I sugar boom briefly brought great wealth to Cuba.
Caribbean.35: The 1920 collapse of sugar prices ruined many Cuban planters, and US companies bought up land. Gerardo Machado became Cuba's strongman in 1925. Jamaican-born Marcus Garvey led a mass movement for Black pride and African unity.
Caribbean.36: Rafael Trujillo seized power in the Dominican Republic in 1930 and ordered the 1937 massacre of thousands of Haitians. In Cuba, Fulgencio Batista rose to power. Labor riots swept the British Caribbean, sparking trade unions and new political parties.
Caribbean.37: German U-boats attacked shipping in the Caribbean during World War II. France's islands became overseas departments in 1946, and Puerto Rico's Operation Bootstrap began rapid industrialization. In 1948, the Windrush brought Caribbean migrants to Britain.
Caribbean.38: Batista seized power in Cuba in 1952, and Fidel Castro's revolution toppled him in 1959. Puerto Rico became a US commonwealth in 1952, and François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier took power in Haiti in 1957. The British islands formed the short-lived West Indies Federation.
Caribbean.39: The US-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba failed in 1961, and the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war. Jamaica and Trinidad became independent in 1962, followed by Barbados. Trujillo was assassinated, and US troops intervened in the Dominican Republic in 1965.
Caribbean.40: More British islands became independent, including the Bahamas and Grenada. Reggae carried Jamaican culture worldwide, and Cuba sent troops to Angola. Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier ruled Haiti, and a leftist revolution took power in Grenada in 1979.
Caribbean.41: The 1980 Mariel boatlift brought about 125,000 Cubans to the US. The US invaded Grenada in 1983, and Haiti's Duvalier dictatorship fell in 1986. Tourism and offshore banking became key industries for many islands.
Caribbean.42: The Soviet Union's collapse plunged Cuba into a severe economic crisis known as the Special Period. Haiti elected Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who was overthrown in 1991 and restored by US troops in 1994. Tourism boomed in the Dominican Republic and elsewhere.
Caribbean.43: Raúl Castro succeeded his brother Fidel in Cuba. Haiti's Aristide was ousted again in 2004, and UN peacekeepers arrived. Venezuela's PetroCaribe program provided cheap oil to many islands, while tourism grew across the region.
Caribbean.44: The 2010 Haiti earthquake killed over 100,000 people, and a cholera outbreak followed. The US and Cuba restored diplomatic relations in 2015. Puerto Rico faced a debt crisis, then devastating Hurricane Maria in 2017.
Caribbean.45: COVID-19 shut down tourism across the islands. Haiti's president was assassinated in 2021 and gangs took over much of Port-au-Prince. Cuba faced protests, blackouts and mass emigration, while Barbados became a republic in 2021.

Central America.0: Paleo-Indian hunters passed through the isthmus on their way into South America by the end of the Ice Age. Afterwards, Archaic foragers lived in its forests and coasts, and in Panama people were already cultivating plants such as squash and arrowroot by c. 7000 BC. Maize arrived from Mexico later.
Central America.1: Archaic peoples lived by foraging, fishing and small-scale gardening. In Panama, Monagrillo pottery, made c. 2500 BC, is among the earliest in the Americas. Communities were small, mobile and organized by kinship, with farming slowly becoming more important.
Central America.2: Farming villages appeared along the Pacific coast of Guatemala, and maize-growing settlers moved into the Maya lowlands toward the end of this era. Pottery and settled life spread through the region. In lower Central America, villages grew around root crops and maize.
Central America.3: Early Maya villages and ceremonial centers took shape in Guatemala and Belize, at sites like Ceibal and Nakbé, where people built the first platforms and plazas. Olmec styles from Mexico influenced local art. Communities were growing more organized and unequal.
Central America.4: Maya communities in the Mirador Basin of northern Guatemala built raised causeways and larger temples. In the highlands, Kaminaljuyu, on the site of today's Guatemala City, grew into a major center. Long-distance trade carried jade and obsidian.
Central America.5: Maya centers like Nakbé and El Mirador grew rapidly, with large stone platforms and plazas. In El Salvador, Chalchuapa thrived on trade. Society was becoming more hierarchical, with chiefs and specialists in crafts and rituals.
Central America.6: The Late Preclassic Maya began building on a monumental scale, especially at El Mirador. Early forms of Maya writing were emerging. Highland centers like Kaminaljuyu controlled trade in obsidian and jade.
Central America.7: El Mirador grew into a huge city with massive pyramids, while other centers spread across the Petén lowlands. Kings began to appear in art, holding religious and political power. The Maya were developing calendars and hieroglyphic writing.
Central America.8: The Preclassic Maya megacity El Mirador reached its peak, with the La Danta pyramid among the largest in the world. At nearby San Bartolo, murals painted c. 100 BC depict Maya myths and kingship. The highland and Pacific coast centers flourished.
Central America.9: El Mirador still dominated the Petén lowlands, linked to other cities by raised causeways. Kaminaljuyu and Takalik Abaj thrived in the highlands and Pacific slope, carving monuments with early writing and dates. Maya kingship was becoming firmly established.
Central America.10: El Mirador began to decline, possibly due to environmental damage and political change. Tikal and other cities were growing. In lower Central America, chiefdoms in Costa Rica and Panama traded jade, pottery and food.
Central America.11: Many Preclassic Maya cities, including El Mirador, were abandoned in a crisis whose causes are still debated, perhaps drought or deforestation. Tikal survived and grew stronger, laying foundations for the Classic era. In the highlands, Kaminaljuyu remained powerful.
Central America.12: The Classic Maya golden age began around c. 250, with dynasties ruling cities such as Tikal. The Maya refined their hieroglyphic writing, calendars, astronomy and use of zero, carving dated stone stelae such as Tikal's Stela 29 in 292.
Central America.13: In 378, warriors linked to Teotihuacan arrived at Tikal and installed a new dynasty, spreading central Mexican influence. Maya city-states grew in number and size. Lower Central American societies were organized as chiefdoms rather than kingdoms.
Central America.14: In 426, K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' founded the royal dynasty of Copán in Honduras. Tikal dominated the central lowlands. The Ilopango volcano in El Salvador erupted massively c. 431, devastating the surrounding region.
Central America.15: Tikal was defeated in 562 by Caracol, in Belize, which was allied with the powerful Calakmul. A long hiatus followed at Tikal. Around c. 600, a volcanic eruption buried the village of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador, preserving everyday Maya life.
Central America.16: Calakmul dominated the Maya world through a network of allied cities, until Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil defeated it in 695. Copán grew wealthy and powerful. Maya art and architecture flourished.
Central America.17: Classic Maya population peaked, possibly in the millions. In 738, Copán's king Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil was captured and executed by Quiriguá. Copán built its great Hieroglyphic Stairway, while Tikal raised new temples.
Central America.18: The Classic Maya collapse swept through the southern lowlands between c. 800 and 900, caused by drought, warfare and overpopulation. Kings stopped erecting monuments and cities like Tikal and Copán were gradually abandoned.
Central America.19: The southern Maya lowlands emptied, and the last Long Count dates were carved. Maya communities survived in smaller villages, around lakes in the Petén and in the Guatemalan highlands. In Costa Rica and Panama, chiefdoms made gold ornaments and stone spheres.
Central America.20: In the Postclassic period, Nahua-speaking Pipil migrants from Mexico settled in El Salvador. Highland Maya peoples like the K'iche' and Kaqchikel formed new kingdoms. Lower Central America saw powerful chiefdoms, with centers like Guayabo in Costa Rica.
Central America.21: Small Maya kingdoms competed in the Guatemalan highlands, building fortified hilltop towns. Pipil communities grew in El Salvador, while chiefdoms flourished in Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Trade linked the region to Mexico and South America.
Central America.22: The K'iche' Maya were emerging as the main power of the Guatemalan highlands. Nahua-speaking Nicarao and Chorotega peoples lived around Nicaragua's lakes. Panama and Costa Rica were home to chiefdoms known for goldwork.
Central America.23: The K'iche' kingdom, ruling from Q'umarkaj (Utatlán), expanded its control over neighboring highland groups. In the Petén, the Itzá Maya ruled from their island capital Nojpetén. Chiefdoms traded gold, cacao and textiles.
Central America.24: The K'iche' kingdom reached its height under K'iq'ab, but the Kaqchikel broke away and founded Iximche c. 1470. Highland Maya kingdoms fought among themselves. Lower Central America's chiefdoms remained independent and prosperous.
Central America.25: Columbus reached the coast in 1502, Balboa crossed Panama to the Pacific in 1513, and Pedro de Alvarado conquered Guatemala in 1524. Disease and enslavement devastated Native peoples. Spain ruled the region from Guatemala, while Panama became a route for Peruvian silver.
Central America.26: The Kingdom of Guatemala exported indigo and cacao, and Spanish landowners relied on Indigenous labor. Pirate Henry Morgan sacked Panama in 1671. The last independent Maya kingdom, the Itzá at Nojpetén, fell to Spain in 1697.
Central America.27: Indigo from El Salvador became the region's main export. British logwood cutters settled in Belize, and the Miskito people allied with Britain on the Caribbean coast. Spanish control of the Caribbean side remained weak.
Central America.28: Earthquakes destroyed Antigua in 1773, and the capital moved to Guatemala City. Bourbon reforms tightened Spanish control. In Belize, British settlers defeated a Spanish attack at St. George's Caye in 1798.
Central America.29: Central America declared independence from Spain in 1821, briefly joined Mexico's empire, and then formed the Federal Republic of Central America (1823 to 1841), uniting Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Panama joined Gran Colombia instead.
Central America.30: The Federal Republic was torn by civil war between liberals led by Francisco Morazán and conservatives led by Rafael Carrera. It broke up into separate states between 1838 and 1841. Coffee cultivation began in Costa Rica.
Central America.31: American adventurer William Walker seized Nicaragua in 1856 but was defeated by Central American armies. The Panama Railroad opened in 1855. Liberal reforms began in Guatemala, and Belize became the colony of British Honduras.
Central America.32: Liberal regimes promoted coffee exports, taking land from Indigenous communities and forcing their labor. Railroads helped US companies start banana plantations. France's attempt to build a Panama canal failed in the 1880s.
Central America.33: Panama split from Colombia in 1903 with US backing, and the US began building the Panama Canal. United Fruit Company gained huge influence, and dictators like Guatemala's Manuel Estrada Cabrera ruled.
Central America.34: The Panama Canal opened in 1914, transforming world shipping and cementing US power in the region. The US occupied Nicaragua from 1912, and banana companies dominated Honduras. The term 'banana republic' captured how foreign firms controlled local politics.
Central America.35: Augusto Sandino led a guerrilla war against US Marines occupying Nicaragua until they withdrew in 1933. United Fruit controlled land, railways and ports in several countries. Coffee and banana prices shaped politics, and a small landowning elite held power.
Central America.36: The Depression brought dictators to power, including Ubico in Guatemala and Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who had Sandino killed. In El Salvador, the army killed thousands of peasants in the 1932 Matanza.
Central America.37: In 1944, a revolution in Guatemala overthrew Ubico and began a decade of democracy. Costa Rica's brief 1948 civil war led to the abolition of its army. Somoza strengthened his family's grip on Nicaragua.
Central America.38: Guatemala's President Árbenz launched land reform that angered United Fruit. In 1954, a CIA-backed coup in Guatemala toppled him. Somoza was assassinated in 1956, but his sons continued ruling Nicaragua.
Central America.39: Guatemala's long civil war began in 1960, pitting leftist guerrillas against the army. The Sandinista guerrilla movement formed in Nicaragua, and a common market boosted regional trade. El Salvador and Honduras fought the brief 'Football War' in 1969.
Central America.40: A 1972 earthquake devastated Managua, and the Somozas' theft of aid fueled anger. The Sandinista revolution of 1979 toppled the dictatorship. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties promised Panama control of its canal.
Central America.41: Brutal civil wars raged in El Salvador and Guatemala, where the army massacred Maya villagers, and in Nicaragua, where US-backed Contras fought the Sandinistas. Archbishop Romero was murdered in 1980. Belize became independent in 1981, and the US invaded Panama in 1989.
Central America.42: Peace accords ended the wars in El Salvador (1992) and Guatemala (1996), and Nicaraguans voted the Sandinistas out in 1990. Hurricane Mitch devastated Honduras and Nicaragua in 1998. In 1999, Panama took full control of the canal.
Central America.43: Street gangs like MS-13 spread violence, especially in El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala. A free trade deal, CAFTA-DR, linked the region to the US. Daniel Ortega returned to power in Nicaragua in 2007, and a coup ousted Honduras's president in 2009.
Central America.44: Violence and poverty drove large migrations north from Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras. Nicaragua's Ortega crushed protests in 2018. Panama's expanded canal opened in 2016, and protests against corruption toppled Guatemala's president in 2015.
Central America.45: El Salvador's President Bukele imprisoned tens of thousands in a crackdown on gangs and made bitcoin legal tender. Ortega ruled Nicaragua with increasing repression. Guatemala elected reformist Bernardo Arévalo, and drought disrupted the Panama Canal in 2023.

Brazil.0: Hunter-gatherers lived in Brazil by at least c. 12,000 years ago, painting caves in the Amazon and the eastern highlands, where the ancient 'Luzia' skeleton was found. Amazonian peoples later began domesticating manioc, coastal groups piled up shell mounds called sambaquis, and pottery at Taperinha is among the Americas' oldest.
Brazil.1: Brazil's peoples lived by foraging, fishing and early gardening. Along the Atlantic coast, sambaqui builders raised huge shell mounds that served as cemeteries and landmarks. In the Amazon, communities tended manioc, peach palm and other useful plants, slowly shaping the forest itself.
Brazil.2: Sambaqui communities along the southern coast built some of their largest shell mounds, a few as tall as 30 meters. In the southwestern Amazon, the ancestors of the Tupi-speaking peoples were living in their homeland. Farming of manioc and other crops spread through the forest.
Brazil.3: Pottery-making and farming villages became more common in the Amazon basin. Sambaqui builders still thrived on the coast, living on fish and shellfish. Brazil was home to many separate peoples speaking languages of the Tupi, Arawak, Carib and Macro-Jê families.
Brazil.4: Amazonian farmers began creating rich, fertile soils called terra preta (dark earth) by mixing charcoal, pottery and waste into the ground. Early pottery cultures appeared on Marajó Island at the mouth of the Amazon. Coastal shell-mound societies continued.
Brazil.5: Villages grew along Amazonian rivers, supported by fishing, turtle farming and gardens on terra preta. Groups speaking Tupi-Guarani languages began gradually expanding outward from the southern Amazon. Life was organized around villages and kinship rather than states.
Brazil.6: Amazonian societies were diverse, ranging from small mobile bands to large riverside villages that lasted for generations. Terra preta deposits grew around these long-lived settlements. On the coast, sambaqui builders continued their traditions of fishing and mound-building.
Brazil.7: In western Amazonia, in today's Acre, people began building large geometric earthworks, ditched circles and squares now called geoglyphs, around this era. They were likely ceremonial spaces. Farming and managed forests supported growing populations.
Brazil.8: Geoglyph-building continued in Acre, and riverside villages expanded along the Amazon and its tributaries. Tupi-Guarani peoples continued slowly migrating, carrying farming and pottery traditions. The coast remained home to shell-mound societies.
Brazil.9: Brazil's many peoples had no single state but lived in a patchwork of villages. Amazonian communities built terra preta soils, cultivated forest orchards and fished the rivers. Pottery styles became more varied and elaborate.
Brazil.10: Large villages flourished along the Amazon, and the Acre geoglyph tradition continued. Tupi-Guarani-speaking groups spread south and east toward the Paraná River and the coast. Life was village-based, with farming, fishing and hunting.
Brazil.11: In the southern highlands, ancestors of today's southern Jê peoples began living in clustered pit houses in araucaria pine forests, eating pine nuts. Amazonian river societies grew larger. Tupi-Guarani migrations continued.
Brazil.12: Amazonian peoples continued to manage the forest, planting useful trees like Brazil nuts and palms. On the coast, sambaqui societies slowly changed as farmers and potters moved in. Large chiefdoms were beginning to emerge in parts of the Amazon.
Brazil.13: Riverside societies in the Amazon grew more complex, with larger villages and wider trade networks. In the south, pit-house villages spread across the highlands. Tupi-Guarani-speaking farmers expanded toward the Atlantic coast.
Brazil.14: The Marajoara mound-builder culture (c. 400 to 1400) emerged on Marajó Island at the Amazon's mouth. Its people built large earthen mounds for homes and burials and made elaborately painted funerary urns. They may have been organized into chiefdoms.
Brazil.15: Marajoara society thrived, with mound villages, fish ponds and polychrome pottery. Elsewhere, Tupi-Guarani peoples continued their migration, and Amazonian river societies grew. Brazil was home to millions of people spread across diverse cultures.
Brazil.16: Marajoara chiefdoms ruled at the mouth of the Amazon, while villages and chiefdoms lined the main river. Terra preta soils supported intensive farming. Shell-mound building was fading on the coast as Tupi farmers arrived.
Brazil.17: Amazonian societies continued to expand, with large settlements on bluffs above the rivers and causeways linking fields and villages. Marajoara culture remained strong at the river's mouth. In the south, Guarani farmers moved along the river valleys, clearing forest gardens.
Brazil.18: In the Upper Xingu region, ancestors of today's Kuikuro people began building villages that would grow into networks of towns. Marajoara and other Amazonian chiefdoms thrived. Tupi-Guarani peoples spread along the coast.
Brazil.19: The Santarém (Tapajós) culture began to rise near the mouth of the Tapajós River, known for intricate pottery. Amazonian chiefdoms controlled stretches of river. Sambaqui building had largely ended on the coast.
Brazil.20: The Santarém culture grew into a powerful chiefdom with a large central town. Marajoara society continued. Tupinambá and other Tupi peoples occupied much of the Atlantic coast, farming manioc and fighting rival groups.
Brazil.21: Amazonian chiefdoms flourished along the main rivers, with dense populations living on terra preta soils. The Santarém culture produced elaborate ceramics and green stone amulets called muiraquitãs. Tupi peoples dominated the coast.
Brazil.22: In the Upper Xingu, villages surrounded by ditches and linked by roads formed 'garden cities' with plazas and bridges. Santarém and other chiefdoms thrived. Brazil's population may have been in the millions.
Brazil.23: Marajoara culture declined by c. 1400. Xingu settlements and Santarém continued to flourish. Tupinambá and Guarani peoples lived in villages of large communal houses along the coast and southern rivers.
Brazil.24: Brazil was home to millions of Native people in hundreds of societies. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, drawn up by Spain and Portugal, gave Portugal the eastern part of South America, even before Europeans had seen it.
Brazil.25: In 1500, Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal. The Portuguese first traded for brazilwood, then built sugar plantations in the northeast worked by enslaved Africans. Salvador became the capital in 1549, while Jesuit missions and epidemics transformed and devastated Native societies.
Brazil.26: The Dutch held the sugar-rich northeast from 1630 to 1654. Palmares, the largest runaway-slave community, resisted for decades until destroyed in the 1690s. Brazil became the largest destination of the slave trade, and bandeirante raiders pushed inland.
Brazil.27: The discovery of gold in Minas Gerais sparked a gold rush, drawing settlers and enslaved Africans inland. Ouro Preto grew rich, building ornate Baroque churches. Diamonds were also found, making Brazil Portugal's most valuable colony.
Brazil.28: Portugal's minister Pombal centralized control, expelled the Jesuits in 1759 and moved the capital to Rio de Janeiro in 1763. Gold output declined. In 1789, a plot for independence in Minas Gerais was crushed, and its leader Tiradentes was executed.
Brazil.29: In 1808, the Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio, making Brazil the center of the empire. In 1822, Prince Pedro declared independence, founding the Empire of Brazil with himself as Emperor Pedro I.
Brazil.30: Brazil lost Uruguay in 1828, and Pedro I abdicated in 1831. During the regency, revolts erupted in several provinces, including the Malê uprising of enslaved Muslims in Bahia. Pedro II took the throne in 1840, and coffee became a key export.
Brazil.31: Brazil ended the Atlantic slave trade in 1850, but slavery continued. Coffee plantations expanded in São Paulo and Rio. Brazil joined Argentina and Uruguay in the brutal Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870), and the 1871 Free Womb Law freed the children of enslaved mothers.
Brazil.32: In 1888, Brazil became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. The army overthrew Pedro II in 1889, creating a republic. Millions of European immigrants arrived, and the Amazon rubber boom made Manaus rich.
Brazil.33: The republic was dominated by coffee planters of São Paulo and Minas Gerais. The Amazon rubber boom peaked, and Brazil acquired Acre from Bolivia in 1903. Rio de Janeiro was rebuilt with grand boulevards.
Brazil.34: The rubber boom collapsed as plantations in Asia took over. Brazil joined World War I in 1917. Industry grew in São Paulo, and the Contestado War pitted peasants against the government in the south.
Brazil.35: Young army officers known as tenentes rebelled against the coffee oligarchy, and the Prestes Column marched across the interior. São Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week launched a new Brazilian culture. The 1929 crash devastated coffee prices and the old republic's finances.
Brazil.36: In 1930, Getúlio Vargas took power in a revolution. In 1937, he imposed the Estado Novo dictatorship, centralizing power and promoting industry and nationalism. He introduced labor laws that won him support among workers.
Brazil.37: Brazil joined the Allies in World War II and sent troops to fight in Italy. Vargas was overthrown in 1945, and a new democratic constitution was adopted in 1946. Industrialization continued, with state-backed steel mills.
Brazil.38: Vargas returned to power by election in 1951 and created the oil company Petrobras, but took his own life in 1954. President Kubitschek promised 'fifty years of progress in five.' Brazil won its first World Cup in 1958.
Brazil.39: In 1960, Brasília became the capital, built from scratch in the interior. Political turmoil led to a military coup in 1964, which began military rule lasting until 1985. The regime increasingly repressed opponents.
Brazil.40: The military regime presided over an 'economic miracle' of rapid growth, while censoring the press and torturing opponents. The Trans-Amazonian Highway opened the rainforest to settlement. Late in the decade, the regime began a slow political opening.
Brazil.41: The debt crisis brought soaring inflation and economic stagnation. Millions joined the Diretas Já campaign demanding direct elections, and democracy was restored in 1985. A new constitution was adopted in 1988, and activist Chico Mendes was killed defending the Amazon.
Brazil.42: President Collor was impeached for corruption in 1992. The 1994 Real Plan ended hyperinflation, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso stabilized the economy and privatized state firms. Brazil hosted the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio, as global attention turned to the Amazon.
Brazil.43: President Lula, a former metalworker, expanded social programs like Bolsa Família that cut poverty. A commodity boom fueled growth, and Brazil joined the BRICS group of emerging powers. Huge offshore oil reserves were discovered.
Brazil.44: Dilma Rousseff faced mass protests, a deep recession and the Car Wash corruption scandal, and was impeached in 2016. Brazil hosted the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics. Jair Bolsonaro won the presidency in 2018.
Brazil.45: COVID-19 killed over 700,000 Brazilians. Lula won the 2022 election, and Bolsonaro supporters stormed government buildings in January 2023. Bolsonaro was later convicted of plotting a coup, and Brazil hosted the COP30 climate summit in 2025.

Andes.0: Hunter-gatherers spread through the Andes by c. 12,000 years ago, adapting to coasts, valleys and high grasslands. Over millennia, Andean peoples domesticated potatoes, squash and beans, and herders tamed llamas and alpacas from wild camelids. In Ecuador, the Valdivia culture made some of the Americas' earliest pottery.
Andes.1: Around c. 2600 BC, Caral in Peru's Norte Chico region became the oldest city in the Americas, with stone pyramids and sunken plazas, sustained by fishing and cotton farming. Valdivia potters in Ecuador and Puerto Hormiga in Colombia made early ceramics. Highland temples like Kotosh appeared.
Andes.2: Norte Chico declined, but large U-shaped temple centers rose on the Peruvian coast, such as Sechín Alto, with carved stones showing warriors and victims. Irrigation farming, pottery and weaving spread. Early metalworkers hammered gold into thin sheets.
Andes.3: The Chavín culture (c. 900 to 200 BC) centered on the temple of Chavín de Huántar in Peru's highlands, a pilgrimage site with stone carvings of jaguars and snakes. Its religious style spread widely. On the south coast, the Paracas culture emerged.
Andes.4: Chavín de Huántar was at its height, drawing pilgrims from far away and spreading a shared religious art. Around Lake Titicaca, villages like Chiripa built sunken temples, and Pukara was emerging. Llama caravans carried goods between coast and highlands.
Andes.5: Chavín influence remained strong across Peru, while the Paracas culture produced fine textiles on the south coast. On the coast of Ecuador and Colombia, the Tumaco-La Tolita culture made remarkable gold and even platinum objects. Societies were increasingly hierarchical.
Andes.6: Paracas weavers produced dazzling embroidered mantles, buried with the dead in large desert cemeteries. Chavín's religious influence started to fade. In the Titicaca basin, Pukara grew into a major ceremonial center with sunken courts and carved stone sculpture.
Andes.7: Chavín's religious influence ended around c. 200 BC, and regional cultures took its place. On the north coast, Salinar and Gallinazo peoples built irrigation canals. Paracas culture flourished on the south coast.
Andes.8: The Nazca culture emerged on Peru's south coast, growing out of Paracas. In Colombia, San Agustín carved large stone statues, and goldworkers in several regions made fine ornaments. The Andes were a patchwork of regional chiefdoms.
Andes.9: Nazca society grew, building the ceremonial center of Cahuachi, a place of pilgrimage. On the north coast, Gallinazo peoples farmed river valleys with canals, and Pukara dominated the Titicaca basin. In Colombia, Calima goldworkers made elaborate ornaments.
Andes.10: Moche society was emerging on Peru's north coast, while Nazca thrived in the south. Both cultures relied on irrigation to farm desert valleys. In Colombia and Ecuador, local chiefdoms produced fine goldwork and pottery.
Andes.11: The Moche of the north coast built huge adobe pyramids, the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, and made realistic portrait pottery. In the south, the Nazca culture made the famous Nazca Lines in the desert. Each culture had its own powerful lords.
Andes.12: Moche lords were buried with rich treasures, such as the Lord of Sipán c. 250. Nazca society continued, with underground aqueducts. In the highlands, the Recuay culture flourished, and Tiwanaku grew on the shores of Lake Titicaca.
Andes.13: The Moche ruled the north coast valleys through powerful warrior-priests who staged ritual combat and sacrifice. Nazca potters made colorful vessels and people kept creating desert lines. Tiwanaku grew into an important city near Lake Titicaca.
Andes.14: Tiwanaku expanded its influence around Lake Titicaca, building monumental stone temples and raised fields that produced large harvests at high altitude. The Moche and Nazca flourished on the coast. In Colombia, many peoples lived in chiefdoms.
Andes.15: Severe floods and droughts, possibly linked to El Niño, disrupted Moche society. Tiwanaku built the Akapana pyramid and expanded its trade networks. In the highlands of Ayacucho, the Wari state was beginning to rise.
Andes.16: The Wari and Tiwanaku empires dominated the central Andes. Wari, based near Ayacucho, built administrative centers and roads that foreshadowed the Inca. Tiwanaku controlled the Titicaca basin and colonies in lower valleys, held together by religion and llama caravans.
Andes.17: Wari expanded its control, building centers like Pikillacta near Cusco. Moche society came to an end, and the Lambayeque (Sicán) culture rose on the north coast. In Colombia, the Muisca and Tairona were forming chiefdoms.
Andes.18: Wari and Tiwanaku remained powerful in the Andes. The Sicán culture flourished on the north coast, known for gold masks and metalwork. In Colombia, the Tairona began building Ciudad Perdida.
Andes.19: Sicán lords built pyramids and buried rulers with vast amounts of gold. Wari began to decline. The Chimú culture was emerging on the north coast, with its capital at Chan Chan.
Andes.20: Wari and Tiwanaku collapsed around c. 1000, possibly due to drought. The Chimú began building Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas. Muisca and Tairona chiefdoms flourished in Colombia, and the Chachapoya built fortresses like Kuélap.
Andes.21: The Chimú expanded along the north coast. Around Lake Titicaca, Aymara kingdoms like the Lupaca and Colla filled the gap left by Tiwanaku. Legend says the Inca founded Cusco around this time.
Andes.22: The Inca were a small kingdom in the Cusco valley, competing with neighbors. The Chimú grew stronger, and the Chincha traders thrived on the south coast. In Colombia, the Muisca formed confederations under rulers called the Zipa and Zaque.
Andes.23: The Chimú conquered the Lambayeque region around c. 1375, building the largest coastal kingdom. In the highlands, the Inca fought rivals like the Chanka. Muisca chiefdoms in Colombia traded gold, salt and emeralds.
Andes.24: In 1438, Pachacuti founded the Inca Empire after defeating the Chanka. The Inca conquered the Chimú and built Machu Picchu c. 1450. Their empire, called Tawantinsuyu, stretched from Ecuador to Chile. In 1498, Columbus reached Venezuela.
Andes.25: An Inca civil war and smallpox (1527 to 1532) weakened the empire. In 1532, Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa and conquered the Inca. Spain founded Lima and Bogotá, and silver from Potosí (from 1545) funded Spain's empire.
Andes.26: The Viceroyalty of Peru ruled from Lima, and Potosí became one of the world's largest cities. Spanish laws forced Indigenous people to labor in mines under the mita system. Cartagena became a major slave port.
Andes.27: Spain created the Viceroyalty of New Granada, centered on Bogotá. Potosí's silver production declined, and Venezuela grew rich from cacao. Indigenous and mixed-race communities resisted heavy taxes and forced labor.
Andes.28: In 1780 to 1781, Túpac Amaru II, claiming Inca descent, led a massive Indigenous rebellion against Spanish abuses that Spain crushed brutally. Túpac Katari besieged La Paz. In New Granada, the Comuneros revolted against taxes, and Creole discontent slowly grew.
Andes.29: Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the independence wars. Between 1819 and 1824, they liberated Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, culminating in the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824. Gran Colombia was formed.
Andes.30: Bolivia became independent in 1825, and Gran Colombia broke into Venezuela, Ecuador and New Granada (Colombia) by 1831. Military strongmen called caudillos ruled. A Peru-Bolivian Confederation failed in 1839, and Peru's guano exports began to boom.
Andes.31: Peru grew rich from guano fertilizer exports, importing Chinese laborers to dig it. Slavery was abolished across the region in the 1850s. Venezuela fought the bloody Federal War, and Colombia adopted a loose federal constitution in 1863.
Andes.32: In the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia, and Bolivia lost its coast. Colombia's Regeneration created a centralized state, and its Thousand Days' War began in 1899.
Andes.33: Colombia's Thousand Days' War ended in 1902, and Panama broke away in 1903. In Venezuela, Juan Vicente Gómez seized power in 1908. Rubber barons brutalized Indigenous workers in the Amazon.
Andes.34: Oil was discovered in Venezuela in 1914, beginning its transformation. Hiram Bingham brought Machu Picchu to world attention in 1911. Augusto Leguía began an eleven-year rule in Peru in 1919.
Andes.35: Venezuela became one of the world's top oil exporters under the dictator Gómez, as foreign companies poured in. Peru's Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre founded the APRA movement. In Colombia, troops killed striking banana workers in 1928.
Andes.36: Bolivia lost the Chaco War (1932 to 1935) against Paraguay, discrediting its old elite. Colombia and Peru fought over Leticia in the Amazon. The Depression hit export economies hard, and new nationalist and reformist movements grew.
Andes.37: Peru defeated Ecuador in a 1941 border war. In Colombia, the 1948 assassination of populist leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán sparked riots in Bogotá and a decade of civil violence known as La Violencia. Venezuela's brief democracy ended in a 1948 coup.
Andes.38: Bolivia's 1952 revolution nationalized tin mines, gave land to peasants and granted universal suffrage. Venezuela's dictator Pérez Jiménez fell in 1958, beginning democracy. In Colombia, the National Front ended La Violencia.
Andes.39: Guerrilla movements like the FARC formed in Colombia. Che Guevara was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Venezuela helped found OPEC in 1960, and a military government took power in Peru in 1968.
Andes.40: Peru's military regime carried out sweeping land reform and nationalizations. Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in 1976 and enjoyed a boom. Bolivia was ruled by a military dictatorship under Hugo Banzer, and Peru returned to civilian rule in 1980.
Andes.41: Peru's Shining Path insurgency killed tens of thousands, and Colombian cocaine cartels like Pablo Escobar's spread terror. Hyperinflation struck Bolivia and Peru, and riots shook Caracas in 1989. In Colombia, a volcanic mudflow buried the town of Armero in 1985.
Andes.42: Peru's Alberto Fujimori captured Shining Path's leader in 1992 but ruled autocratically. Escobar was killed in 1993. In 1999, Hugo Chávez took power in Venezuela and launched his 'Bolivarian revolution.'
Andes.43: Chávez used oil wealth for social programs while concentrating power. Evo Morales became Bolivia's first Indigenous president in 2006, and Rafael Correa rose in Ecuador. Colombia's army, backed by the US, pushed back the FARC.
Andes.44: After Chávez's death in 2013, Venezuela collapsed under Nicolás Maduro, with hyperinflation and shortages, and some 7 million or more people emigrated. The 2016 Colombia-FARC peace deal ended a 52-year war. Bolivia's Evo Morales was ousted in 2019.
Andes.45: COVID-19 hit Peru with one of the world's highest death rates, and Peru cycled through presidents. Maduro claimed victory in Venezuela's disputed 2024 election. Gustavo Petro became Colombia's first leftist president, and gang violence surged in Ecuador.

Southern Tip.0: Around c. 14,500 years ago, people camped at Monte Verde in southern Chile, an early human site in the Americas. Hunters later pursued horses and giant sloths in Patagonia and stenciled hands at Cueva de las Manos, and by c. 5000 BC the Chinchorro of the Atacama coast made the world's oldest artificial mummies.
Southern Tip.1: Chinchorro fishing communities on the Atacama coast continued their elaborate mummification. Guanaco hunters roamed Patagonia and the Pampas, while canoe peoples fished and hunted seals in the channels of Tierra del Fuego. In Uruguay's wetlands, people began building earthen mounds called cerritos.
Southern Tip.2: Mound-building communities in Uruguay grew plants such as squash and maize alongside fishing and hunting. The Chinchorro tradition faded around c. 1500 BC. In the Atacama and northwest Argentina, people began herding llamas and farming in oases.
Southern Tip.3: Formative farming villages appeared in the Atacama Desert and northwest Argentina, with sites like Tulor near San Pedro de Atacama. Llama caravans linked oases and highlands. Further south, hunter-gatherers still lived in Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego.
Southern Tip.4: Northern farmers grew maize, beans and quinoa, irrigating desert valleys. Mound-builders lived in Uruguay's wetlands, while hunter-gatherer bands roamed the Pampas and Patagonia. No states existed; people lived in villages or mobile groups.
Southern Tip.5: Villages in northwest Argentina produced fine pottery and carved stone objects. Canoe peoples in Tierra del Fuego developed a culture well suited to the cold seas. Patagonian hunters followed guanaco herds across the steppes.
Southern Tip.6: Farming communities expanded in northwest Argentina, and pottery styles became more elaborate. In central Chile, foragers and early farmers lived along the rivers. The south remained the land of hunter-gatherers.
Southern Tip.7: In northwest Argentina, the Tafí culture raised standing stones and terraced fields in mountain valleys. Atacama villages traded with the highlands. Mound-builders and hunter-gatherers lived in the east and south.
Southern Tip.8: Agricultural villages in northwest Argentina grew in size and complexity, including the Ciénaga culture. Herders in the Atacama exchanged goods across the Andes. Elsewhere, people lived as hunters, fishers and foragers.
Southern Tip.9: Village life deepened in the north, with metal objects starting to appear. In Uruguay and southern Brazil, mound-builders continued their traditions. Patagonia and the Pampas were home to mobile hunting peoples.
Southern Tip.10: Northern farmers continued irrigating fields, and copper and gold were being worked in the Andean foothills. In south-central Chile, the ancestors of the Mapuche were beginning to farm and make pottery. Hunter-gatherers lived throughout the south.
Southern Tip.11: The Ciénaga culture flourished in northwest Argentina, producing fine engraved pottery and early metalwork. Mapuche ancestors lived in the forests of south-central Chile. During the first millennium AD, Guarani-speaking farmers spread into the Paraná and Paraguay river basins.
Southern Tip.12: Pitrén pottery appeared in south-central Chile among early Mapuche communities, who combined gardening with gathering and hunting. The Atacama oases grew more populous. Patagonian and Fuegian peoples continued their hunting and fishing ways, adapted to cold steppes and seas.
Southern Tip.13: Farming and herding villages flourished in the north, linked by caravan routes across deserts and mountains. Guarani farmers settled in the forests of Paraguay, growing manioc and maize. The Pampas and Patagonia remained hunting lands for mobile bands.
Southern Tip.14: The rising power of Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, influenced San Pedro de Atacama through trade and religion. Villages in northwest Argentina grew larger. The region had no large states, and most people lived in villages or mobile bands.
Southern Tip.15: Tiwanaku trade brought fine textiles, pottery and carved snuff trays to the Atacama oases, where local leaders gained status. Guarani villages spread along the Paraná River. Hunter-gatherers continued their ancient ways across the Pampas and Patagonia.
Southern Tip.16: The Aguada culture emerged in northwest Argentina, with powerful leaders and art featuring jaguars, warriors and sacrifice. Tiwanaku's influence remained strong in the Atacama. Mapuche ancestors farmed and foraged in the forests of south-central Chile.
Southern Tip.17: Aguada flourished, building ceremonial centers and producing fine bronze metalwork and painted pottery. Tiwanaku trade connected the region to the central Andes. Guarani farmers continued expanding through the river forests of Paraguay and beyond.
Southern Tip.18: Aguada remained powerful in northwest Argentina, its society divided between elites and farmers. In south-central Chile, Mapuche communities farmed and gathered pine nuts. Patagonian peoples continued to hunt guanaco and rhea across the open steppe.
Southern Tip.19: Aguada declined around c. 900, and new regional chiefdoms emerged in northwest Argentina. The Atacama oases faced change as Tiwanaku weakened. Guarani communities thrived in Paraguay, while Charrúa and other hunters roamed Uruguay's grasslands.
Southern Tip.20: With Tiwanaku's collapse, fortified villages called pucaras appeared in the Atacama and northwest Argentina, reflecting increased conflict among local groups. The Diaguita culture flourished in north-central Chile, known for its painted pottery. Mapuche groups lived in the south.
Southern Tip.21: Regional chiefdoms competed in northwest Argentina, building walled settlements on hillsides with terraced fields. The Diaguita prospered in Chile's transverse valleys. Mapuche communities lived in villages scattered across the forests and rivers of the south.
Southern Tip.22: Settlements like Quilmes in northwest Argentina grew into large stone towns with thousands of people. Pucaras dominated the Atacama landscape. Charrúa hunters lived in Uruguay, Guarani farmers in Paraguay, and nomadic bands across the Pampas and Patagonia.
Southern Tip.23: The Diaguita, Atacameño and Calchaquí peoples ruled their own valleys and oases. Guarani villages were densely populated along the rivers. Mapuche society was organized into kin-based groups without a central ruler, a structure that later made them hard to conquer.
Southern Tip.24: The Inca expanded into northern Chile and Argentina in the late 1400s, building roads and forts. The Mapuche resisted, stopping the Inca at the Maule River. Patagonia remained beyond Inca reach.
