Southern Tip.25: In 1520, Magellan passed the strait that bears his name. Spain founded Asunción (1537), Santiago (1541) and Buenos Aires (refounded in 1580). The Mapuche resisted Spain in the Arauco War, killing the conqueror Pedro de Valdivia in 1553.
Southern Tip.26: Spain ruled from Santiago, Buenos Aires and Asunción, but the Mapuche held the land south of the Bío-Bío River. Jesuits organized Guarani missions in Paraguay, and Buenos Aires grew through smuggling. Wild cattle multiplied on the Pampas.
Southern Tip.27: Spain founded Montevideo in the 1720s to counter Portuguese expansion. Jesuit missions thrived, and cattle hides became key exports. In Paraguay, settlers revolted against colonial authorities in the Comuneros revolt.
Southern Tip.28: Spain created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776, centered on Buenos Aires. The Jesuits were expelled in 1767, and Guarani communities fought the Guarani War (1754 to 1756). Trade reforms boosted Buenos Aires.
Southern Tip.29: British invasions of Buenos Aires were defeated in 1806 and 1807. Paraguay won independence in 1811, Argentina declared it in 1816, and San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817 to liberate Chile by 1818.
Southern Tip.30: Uruguay became independent in 1828 as a buffer between Argentina and Brazil. Juan Manuel de Rosas ruled Argentina as a strongman, while Chile's Diego Portales built a stable conservative state. Britain seized the Falkland Islands in 1833.
Southern Tip.31: Rosas fell in 1852, and Argentina adopted a constitution in 1853. The Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870) devastated Paraguay, which lost much of its male population. Chile grew wealthy through copper and wheat.
Southern Tip.32: Argentina's 'Conquest of the Desert' seized Patagonia from Indigenous peoples, and Chile occupied Mapuche lands. Mass European immigration transformed Argentina and Uruguay, while Chile won nitrate-rich lands in the War of the Pacific.
Southern Tip.33: Argentina became one of the world's richest countries, exporting beef and grain. Uruguay's José Batlle y Ordóñez began building a welfare state. Chile's nitrate wealth was shaken by strikes, including the 1907 Iquique massacre.
Southern Tip.34: Argentina's 1912 Sáenz Peña Law introduced secret, compulsory male suffrage, bringing Hipólito Yrigoyen's Radicals to power in 1916. Uruguay expanded social reforms. Chile's nitrate exports suffered from new synthetic fertilizers, and Argentina's 1919 Tragic Week saw workers killed.
Southern Tip.35: Argentina prospered on beef and grain exports, but striking ranch workers in Patagonia were massacred by the army. Chile's nitrate industry declined, and Carlos Ibáñez ruled as a strongman from 1927. Uruguay remained a stable democracy.
Southern Tip.36: A 1930 coup in Argentina began the 'Infamous Decade' of military-backed rule. Uruguay hosted and won the first World Cup in 1930. Paraguay defeated Bolivia in the Chaco War (1932 to 1935).
Southern Tip.37: In 1946, Juan Perón was elected president of Argentina, and with his wife Eva he built a powerful movement based on workers and nationalism. Chile's Gabriela Mistral won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1945, and Chilean women gained the vote in 1949.
Southern Tip.38: Perón was overthrown in 1955, and Argentina alternated between weak civilian governments and military rule. Alfredo Stroessner seized power in Paraguay in 1954, beginning a 35-year dictatorship. Chile and Uruguay remained democracies, though Uruguay's economy stagnated.
Southern Tip.39: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile was the strongest ever recorded. Argentina suffered repeated military coups, and the 1969 Cordobazo uprising shook its regime. Uruguay's Tupamaro guerrillas grew active, and Chile's Eduardo Frei began land reform.
Southern Tip.40: Socialist Salvador Allende was elected in Chile in 1970, but the 1973 Pinochet coup began a brutal dictatorship. Uruguay also fell to military rule, and Argentina's 'Dirty War' (1976 to 1983) disappeared thousands.
Southern Tip.41: Argentina's defeat in the 1982 Falklands War brought down its junta, and Argentine democracy returned in 1983. Uruguay's democracy returned in 1985, Stroessner fell in 1989, and Chilean democracy was restored in 1990.
Southern Tip.42: Under Carlos Menem, Argentina pegged its peso to the dollar and privatized industries, taming inflation. The Mercosur trade bloc formed in 1991. Chile's economy grew fast under restored democracy, and Pinochet was arrested in London in 1998.
Southern Tip.43: Argentina's economy collapsed in 2001, leading to default and political chaos, before recovering under the Kirchners. Michelle Bachelet became Chile's first female president in 2006. Left-leaning governments rose in Uruguay and Paraguay.
Southern Tip.44: Uruguay legalized marijuana in 2013 under José Mujica. Argentine Jorge Bergoglio became Pope Francis in 2013. Chile rescued 33 trapped miners in 2010, but in 2019 mass protests erupted against inequality.
Southern Tip.45: Chile's voters rejected two proposed new constitutions in 2022 and 2023. Argentina won the 2022 World Cup and elected libertarian Javier Milei in 2023, who imposed sweeping austerity. Pope Francis died in 2025.
